en: In this key, the rise in prices is compatible with a rentier rationality of maximizing dividends through markups defined by the intermediary's structural position, draining income through subscriptions, fees and access “rights”, which explains the author's refusal of the conventional monetary diagnosis and his direct criticism of the Central Bank's justifications: “It is not demand inflation, and the Central Bank's justifications […] are simply false”. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 70)</2>.

The expression “mandatory intermediary” describes, in Dowbor, the shift from competition by product to competition by infrastructural position: rentier gain stabilizes when critical layers of circulation, computing and intermediation become unavoidable points of passage, shifting the dispute to control of access. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 31)</2>.
The Amazon case illustrates this conversion of internal capacity into a generalized toll: “AWS as well as FBA are […] infrastructure rentiers.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

This position is sustained by technical and economic barriers to replication: “Amazon controls critical infrastructures […] in ways that it would be difficult for new interested parties (entrants) to replicate or try to confront with competition.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

The relevant legal point is that intermediation ceases to be a mere “neutral” provision and comes to operate as unilateral governance of the point of passage, with effects on continuity, conditions of permanence and the power to impose recurring costs in dependent digital ecosystems. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31)</2>.

Dowbor offers a systemic frame for contemporary rentierism by emphasizing the mismatch between the digital economic base and institutions still organized by categories of the previous period, which contributes to the persistence of extraction mechanisms that are barely intelligible in the public sphere <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 8; p. 13)</2>.

In Dowbor, the “capture of flows” designates the transformation of digital circulation into a continuous economic asset: payments, data, attention and decisions cease to be side effects of use and come to form part of a measurable and monetizable flow, whose extraction depends on retaining enjoyment within controlled layers (accounts, permissions, proprietary standards, terms of use and curation), reducing the possibility of relevant use outside the governed perimeter <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-31)</2>.

The category reinforces that the consumption of IOC takes place as administered and continuously modulable access, and that the opacity of how this retention works projects duties of transparency and loyalty onto the material shaping of the offer (CDC), especially when legal-technical fences (including IP) are coupled to the perimeter to stabilize the capture <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 19-21; p. 28-31)</2>.

This command becomes capillary because “algorithms and artificial intelligence allow a capillarity that reaches every individual in the world” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>, shifting “consent” to a function that is above all ratifying of an arrangement already implemented, as can be glimpsed in the ordinary experience of compulsoriness: “I cannot move unless I am authorizing some network to install cookies all the time” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</4>.

In this key, the contract tends to operate as a subsequent discursive stabilization of a control already inscribed in the code, including in the administration of “access codes” and in the “management of contents” as structuring dimensions of the platform <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</2>.

When this practical normativity is articulated with technical fences and exclusivity regimes, the closing of access must be read in light of internal limits of legitimacy, above all when the effective teleology of the design shifts to a precarious and revocable toll regime over the enjoyment of IOCs <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 40)</2>.

According to Dowbor, the “nebulous reality” is not a spontaneous information deficit, but an institutional effect of the increasing complexity of contemporary mediations for the appropriation of surplus, which makes them less intelligible and, therefore, less politicizable and attributable in common sense <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</2>.

The consequence is a practical blockage of collective response, associated with the picture of “institutional impotence”: “The institutional impotence we face leads us to a disastrous systemic disarticulation” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</2>.

At the same time, the author refuses to naturalize this opacity as a technical fatality and makes its disputable character explicit when he states: “The present book seeks to make visible and understandable how the mechanisms work today” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3)</2>.

In the sphere of consumption on platforms, this nebulousness reinforces the insufficiency of a merely formal transparency: the availability of terms, policies and documents does not eliminate the practical unintelligibility of the mechanism that organizes the capture and the toll embedded in the experience, which puts pressure on the reading of the duties of information, clarity and objective good faith in the CDC <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</2>.

The formula “owner of a process” is used by Dowbor to indicate that, in digital rentierism, capture ceases to depend on the alienation of a good and comes to stabilize through continued control of the conditions of use, converting enjoyment into authorized permanence within a governed circuit <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

In this key, the relevant economic object is not a “content” in itself, but the very operation of access — its permissions, compatibilities and criteria of continuity —, so that use becomes structurally conditional and subject to unilateral revisions <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

The consequence is that the guarantees intuitively associated with acquisition lose practical density: availability, continuity and power of enjoyment come to depend on the holder of the infrastructure and on the private rules that administer the process <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

The architecture of access and enjoyment designates the set of technical-operational layers that sustain the utility of IOCs over time — code updates, authentication, server availability, compatibilities and integrations — and that therefore shift consumption from the logic of the delivery of a good to continuous participation in a governed process <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>.

In Dowbor, this mutation is described as an institutional passage from the regime of producers and buyers to that of suppliers and users and as the replacement of concrete property by the recurring control of a process, in which economic capture is achieved by charging for use <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

Since enjoyment depends on these layers under the supplier's command, unilateral changes in maintenance, compatibility or access parameters may reconfigure the functional value delivered to the consumer — by degradation, locking or discontinuity — without the phenomenon being adequately captured by the classical categories of acquisition and permanence of the good <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>.

The reference to the conditions of possibility aims only to clarify that the enjoyment of the immaterial depends on the supplier's infrastructural dominion over the practical regimes of access and circulation, so that the consumer's experience is structured by permissions and mediations controlled by the offeror — that is, by the administration of “access codes” and by the “management of contents” as material dimensions of supply <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40)</2>.

For Dowbor, the rentier enjoyment of the digital tends to be organized as authorized permanence in a process: access is continuously conditionable and revisable by the holder of the infrastructure, instead of ending in the classical logic of the delivery of a good <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

This precariousness does not designate an episodic failure, but a functional trait of the arrangement, since the supplier preserves the capacity to restrict, reconfigure or end the experience through the administrative modulation of permissions, normalizing social life as a circuit of passage and recurring charges: “Living ceases to be a stroll […] to become a permanent race from toll to toll.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

Let us close the beaches, then. […] we are increasingly trapped in the race to increase our monthly income, without which we will find ourselves deprived of a series of essential services.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

Within the scope of the CDC, this reinforces that signs of “service”, “plan” and “purchase” may mask a structurally revocable enjoyment, raising opacity and making it difficult, in practice, to anticipate and contest relevant changes in the conditions of use <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

It is in this sense that the author describes the corporate hardening of control as a “strategy implemented through a series of new laws intended to extend the copyright term of the work, reinforce criminal penalties for infringing copyright, and to punish the use of technologies that tried to avoid the digital obstacles placed on digital content” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 42-43)</2>.

The institutional effect is to convert the ordinary reproducibility of the digital into conditioned circulation: exclusion — through reinforced technical-legal fences — becomes the condition of possibility of the toll, that is, of the income extracted through control of access, and not through the social utility of dissemination <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22; p. 41; p. 51-52)</2>.

The “black box regime”, in the reading proposed from Dowbor, designates an institutional form of opacity in which relevant decisions are shifted to proprietary layers of calculation and organization — ranking, eligibility, visibility, balancing and availability — outside the user's ordinary intelligibility, in an environment marked by algorithmic capillarity and by the orientation of processing toward maximizing economic return <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

The practical consequence is evidentiary and cognitive: the consumer has neither understandable traces nor a common language to reconstruct the effective criteria for modulating the service, although they experience its effects directly in enjoyment <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

In such a context, even when formal terms and documents are available, transparency may remain insufficient for control and attribution, since the relevant decision-making mechanism remains unintelligible — a point that connects to the diagnosis of complexity and opacity and to the insufficiency of merely formal transparency <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 3; p. 13)</2>.

Dowbor formulates the “inverted political sign” as a thesis of institutional reversibility: the same technical base that today sustains draining and enclosure can be organized for purposes of well-being and democratization, because the decisive vector is not “technology” in itself, but the arrangement of incentives and governance that structures access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 82)</2>.

The contrast appears when the author observes that, while technique makes cultural goods more accessible, “the laws […] evolve symmetrically to make access ever more difficult”, shifting the conflict to the legal-institutional discipline of enclosure <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 42)</2>.
Hence the conclusion that the “right of access to knowledge” becomes an axis of economic democratization <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 65)</2>.

This diagnosis finds a parallel in the treatment of network infrastructures and situations without effective competition, in which “private property and ‘economic freedom’, when there is no competition, lead to abuses”, that is, “it is private property, but not a market”, with loss of public purpose <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 31-32)</2>.

The frame supports reading the consumer protection discipline as bearing on the material shaping of the offer and of enjoyment in governed ecosystems, under requirements of transparency and loyalty compatible with the practical difficulty of reconciling profit and social purpose in hybrid structures <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 87)</2>.

Instead of price and conditions presenting themselves as public and comparable attributes of the offer, they become variables calculable per user, modulated by behavioral and socioeconomic inferences oriented toward maximizing return <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 28-29)</2>.

The Serasa example works as an institutionalized illustration of this rationality by recording that “your cost of credit will be adjusted according to the bank's interests”, showing that calibration may exploit information asymmetries and estimated needs, and not merely reflect “risk” in a neutral sense <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29)</2>.

In Dowbor's diagnosis, unproductive rentierism has a distributive expression when the link of proportionality between productive contribution and enrichment is broken, consolidating itself as a drain of social wealth in favor of rentier positions; this shift, for the author, marks the passage of the axis from capital accumulation to the logic of unproductive rentierism <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 13; p. 20)</2>.

The expression “communication corrals”, used by Dowbor, designates the infrastructural closing by which private operators come to control the conditions of access and circulation on the information highways themselves, consolidating the power to select, condition and administer enjoyment in proprietary environments <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49-50)</2>.

This closing is not reducible to a neutral technical option, because it involves the coordinated appropriation of layers ranging from “physical infrastructure” to “codes” and “contents”, shifting the governance of the informational space to private regimes of passage <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 49)</2>.

In an economic key, the “corrals” operate as the condition of possibility of recurring charges for access and permanence, since they transform circulation into an administered crossing and, therefore, one compatible with the toll rationality that runs through the diagnosis of contemporary rentierism <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 49-50)</2>.

The design can be read as compatible with the logic of toll and repeated micro-extraction described by Dowbor, insofar as it brings payment closer to a regime of small continuous captures that are barely salient to the individual <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 29; p. 21)</2>.

When this closed circuit is combined with technical and contractual restrictions on circulation, the governance of access through turnstiles and crossing costs is reinforced, the core of the diagnosis of toll and disproportionate extraction <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 21; p. 39)</2>.
Thus, the informational rentierism described by Dowbor <1>(2024)</1> finds its microarchitectural correlate in the everyday life of platforms.

Intellectual property ceases to operate merely as an incentive and comes to form part of an arrangement of enclosure, functioning as a true “legal latifundium” that immobilizes accumulated technologies and knowledge under titles of prolonged exclusivity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>.

When this latifundium is coupled to license agreements, accounts, DRM, catalogs and authentication mechanisms, the incentive to creation gives way to a technology of blocking and the purpose of copyright comes to operate as a mechanism for closing access, transforming access into a conditional license and enjoyment into a precarious authorization, continuously reconfigurable, insofar as circulation comes to be treated as infringement <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>.

The consequence, in the sphere of consumption, is that what gives concreteness to the consumer's right is not the possession of bits, but the legal materiality of the object, understood as the stability and predictability of the practical conditions that make enjoyment possible over time, in an environment in which economic control shifts from the good to the process and utility depends on continuous governance under private dominion <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

This is institutional concreteness, since the infrastructure and the mechanisms that sustain access, circulation and continuity remain under the control of platforms and their governance systems <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8; p. 51-52)</2>.

The decisive economic point is that, in the immaterial, reproducibility would tend to dissolve price, and this inversion is particularly sensitive in the network environment, because copying is not a deviation, but an ordinary technical condition of enjoyment itself, insofar as copying is part of transmission, storage, caching and, in a certain sense, reading itself <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

By legally requalifying this constitutive gesture, intellectual property ceases to operate merely as an incentive and comes to function as a technology of blocking, since it transforms circulation into infringement and enjoyment into authorization, allowing the supplier to govern the experience of the IOC as precarious and modulable access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51)</2>.

The economic centrality of this surplus is described by Dowbor when he follows Gorz in the analysis of the brand, advertising and symbolic values as the basis of a new formation of value <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2>.

Dowbor associates the problem of Intellectual Property not only with the existence of the right itself, but with its historical extension through organized pressure, observing that “we will only have digital access to a work 70 years after the author's death” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2> and questioning whether very long copyrights and “indefinitely extended” rights are disseminating culture or, on the contrary, stalling the social process <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</4>.

The argument is one of political economy, since, if the realization of profit is mostly concentrated in the first years of commercial exploitation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>, maintaining exclusivity for decades operates as income without a proportional incentivizing function and imposes a massive social cost on research and creative reuse to sustain concentrated private flows.
The author, as the subject of intellectual creation, has little to do with this dynamic, since the rights almost always belong to intermediaries <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>.

Dowbor makes explicit that the proliferation and overlapping of IP rights may produce prohibitive transaction costs and block subsequent innovations by “placing multiple obstacles” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 47)</2>, configuring a tragedy of the anticommons.

The thesis is anchored in examples that make explicit the social materiality of this blocking, citing the “disaster of access to vaccines during Covid-19” as evidence of the patent latifundium <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

Mention is also made of the attempt to patent the “one-click” mechanism as a deliberate gesture to prevent the dissemination of a basic organizational improvement <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 22-23)</2>.
In this process, availability, compatibility and continuity depend on external controls under the supplier's dominion <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 40; p. 51-52)</2>.

The architecture of cumulative permissions comes close to the diagnosis that tangles of legal restrictions and transaction costs may produce underuse and blockages through an excess of vetoes, to the detriment of recombination and subsequent innovation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44; p. 47)</2>, and helps explain why economic activity comes to depend on persistent legal mediations even in trivial operations of production and circulation <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 45-46)</4>.

For this reason, he reaffirms public access to knowledge as a structuring vector, maintaining that knowledge generated with public resources must be socially accessible and serve the common good, and that access to knowledge and connectivity today constitutes a fundamental human right <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 62)</2>.

In the same sense, he states that copyright must be limited, since the purpose of copyright is to ensure reasonable remuneration to the author, and not to guarantee permanent income to the intermediary, which is why he proposes a temporal limitation, even on the order of five years <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

Intermediaries and chains of exploitation remain remunerable, but capture must occur through mechanisms compatible with circulation and access, and not through permanent tolls <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 64)</2>.

On the contrary, he recognizes the historical legitimacy of the incentive, understood as privileged remuneration of the inventor or the author, so as to stimulate scientific and cultural advances <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

In this key, patents and copyrights cease to operate predominantly as a temporary technique of stimulus and come to function as a mechanism of blocking and toll over knowledge, including when effective ownership shifts to intermediaries and economic groups <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36; p. 43; p. 46)</2>.
The intellectual property right is not based on a natural right of property, but on its potential to stimulate future creativity <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

It follows that the hypertrophy of duration and scope produces a teleological mismatch and requires proportionality control when exclusivity becomes autonomous from the incentive and comes to operate as a fence <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

The metaphor of the “legal latifundium”, in Dowbor, describes a teleological dysfunction internal to the Intellectual Property regime: situations in which exclusivity, through hypertrophy of scope, duration and chains of licenses, ceases to operate predominantly as a temporary technique for stimulating future creativity and comes to function as a mechanism for the artificial retention of social utility and for charging tolls on access, recombination and dissemination of technically reproducible knowledge <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44-45)</2>.

For this reason, the critique does not deny IP as a legal technique, but leads its legitimacy back to the purposive foundation that the author makes explicit: “The intellectual property right is not based on the natural right of property, but on its potential to stimulate future creativity.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

The dysfunction worsens when appropriation systematically shifts from the creator to intermediaries, composing the figure of the “absentee owner”: “Copyrights are largely taken over by those who hold the copyright or the patents, and in this case they are almost always intermediaries.” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

In this scenario, the title of exclusivity tends to operate as an economic and institutional bottleneck in the final product, conditioning subsequent trajectories of innovation and access on private control of permissions and licenses, with potential for disproportionate enrichment by position in the circuit <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48-49; p. 58)</2>.

In Dowbor, “fence” designates the teleological inflection in which copyright ceases to operate predominantly as an incentive and comes to function as a perimeter barring access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>, articulating itself with the general mechanism of converting the reproducibility of the immaterial into monetizable artificial scarcity, that is, transforming technical abundance into rarefaction by institutional decision <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</4>.

The utility of the immaterial object depends on the governed continuity of access and on the stability of the technical-organizational rules that structure availability, compatibility and modification, and not on the digital medium itself <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

The structural point is that this stability is anchored in infrastructures under private control, so that the “productive infrastructure […] is controlled by platforms, computers, algorithms and artificial intelligence”. <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 8)</2>.

For this reason, the instability of these rules reconfigures, in practice, the functional value delivered to the consumer and makes enjoyment dependent on continuous governance in process <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 51-52)</2>.

Dowbor situates the corresponding shift when following Gorz, recording that “Gorz naturally moves on to analyze the function of the brand, advertising, symbolic values as the basis of the new formation of value” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2> and that, in the contemporary mutation, “The theory of value, the basis of economic science, shifts” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</4>, toward a regime in which exchange value is anchored “mainly, by its content of knowledge, information, general intelligence” <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</6>.

In this key, the institutional problem is not the existence of symbolic circulation in itself, but the possibility of its capture by contractual and IP fences and by asymmetric governance of visibility and access, reconverting diffuse contribution into an exclusive asset and recurring income; the logic of the “bottleneck” and the “toll” falling on socially cumulative accumulations provides the structural model of this appropriation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 48-49)</2>.

In this hypothesis, the user's contribution ceases to operate as a communal element densifying enjoyment and comes to be requalified as a proprietary input, articulating itself with Dowbor's diagnosis of the reorganization of value formation around brand, advertising and symbolic values <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 23)</2> and of the dependence, in the immaterial, on institutional mechanisms blocking dissemination to stabilize monetization <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 41)</4>.

If exclusivity is legitimized by its instrumental function of stimulating future creativity, extending control beyond the typical period of return on investment tends to reduce the marginal gain of incentive and to operate as continued income by position <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

In the case of copyright, the author observes that the realization of profits is concentrated in the first cycles of exploitation, whereas legal exclusivity may last for decades, converting the remaining protection into a barrier to access, with relevant social costs for cultural dissemination, recombination and licensing, without proportional benefit in new creations <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>.

This asymmetry reinforces the need to read the social function of IP, in platform environments, as a criterion for containing enclosures that come to operate as a toll on technically facilitated circulation, shifting the discussion from the isolated “title” to the institutional architecture that produces blocking, opacity and capture of value in the intangible <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43; p. 46)</2>.

Dowbor draws on Boyle's synthesis to record this effect as a “tragedy of the anticommons”, associating it with the transaction costs generated by a “myriad” of property rights and with the result of restricting innovation by placing multiple obstacles in the path of subsequent developments <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 47)</2>, a diagnosis reinforced by the idea that the “tangle of legal restrictions” may reach a point at which it “hinders more than it stimulates research” <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</4>.

The “patent latifundium” makes it possible to show, by way of example, the loss of proportionality between exclusivity and the corresponding social benefit when barriers persist even under collective urgency: in Dowbor's diagnosis, the “disaster of access to vaccines during Covid-19” exposes how patents can “immobilize” essential technology and organize a “war to make access difficult” as an income mechanism, including under shareholder pressure for dividends to the detriment of access pacts <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36; p. 54)</2>.

The usefulness of the example lies in showing that exclusivity may become autonomous from its justification and operate as a social and economic toll on dissemination, access and public response capacity, restoring the social function of IP as a criterion of institutional limitation and calibration <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 46)</2>.

Dowbor, on the one hand, observes that “openness itself has become a powerful (and impressively beneficial) incentive” <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 38)</2> and, on the other, maintains that remuneration can be organized at another point in the economic chain, preventing long and hypertrophied exclusivities from turning into a permanent toll <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 64)</4>.

On this horizon, various legally accommodable institutional arrangements appear, including funding policies and public procurement, in which remuneration occurs through distributive and public policy mechanisms, consistent with the role of collectively funded basic science and with the circulation of the result as a common good without prejudice to payment for creative work <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 6; p. 39)</2>; remunerated compulsory licenses and sectoral flexibilities as an exceptional technique to overcome bottlenecks and enable technology transfer in the face of global challenges, including with solutions such as pools and access-oriented flexibilities <3>Dowbor</3><4>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 53)</4>; and open licensing models and collective forms of management, which reduce transaction costs and avoid systemic blockages by shifting remuneration to services, curation, maintenance and complementary activities <5>Dowbor</5><6>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43-44; p. 64)</6>.

Taken together, the instruments show that IP, read through its social function, admits degrees of exclusivity and instruments of teleological correction when hypertrophied exclusivity comes to operate as a structural barrier to cultural circulation, recombination and public access <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43-44; p. 64)</2>.

Dowbor recognizes the historical justification of intellectual protection as a technique of incentive — privileged remuneration of the inventor and the author to stimulate scientific and cultural advances —, but maintains that, in the contemporary configuration, patents and copyrights tend to operate as a rentier mechanism of charging for access and blocking the dissemination of knowledge <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

The author exemplifies the dysfunction by the temporal inadequacy of the patent in the face of the technological pace, pointing to the experience of the Covid-19 pandemic as a case of socially disastrous restriction of access, and by the expansion of copyright with economic concentration in publishers, not in authors, illustrating with the horizon of open access to the works of Paulo Freire only in 2067 <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

In this diagnosis, the “war to make access difficult” becomes a central axis of the knowledge economy, while openness mechanisms (Open Access, Creative Commons and the like) appear as an institutional alternative capable of radically expanding worldwide access to knowledge without depending on retention as the ordinary form of remuneration <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>.

The notion of “cybervulnerability” records, with good sensitivity, that cyberspace aggravates already known vulnerabilities and widens the power gap between consumer and supplier, including through factors such as insufficient literacy, informational asymmetry, data collection and manipulation of will <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 86; p. 93; p. 97; p. 120; p. 83-84)</2>.

The author even seeks juridicization through the CDC and the Constitution, which shows a serious effort at normativity, but still coexists with a strong dependence on “cyberspace” as the structural axis of the formulation <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 93; p. 113; p. 119)</2>.

Along these lines, the author defines “cybervulnerability” as “the hypervulnerability of the consumer caused by the greater fragility of this subject in consumer relations established in cyberspace given the existence of more uncertainties, risks and occurrences of harm in this environment, which increases the power gap between the consumer and the supplier” <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 86)</2>.

Acosta maintains that cybervulnerability results from the “aggravation of the consumer's vulnerability(ies) caused by the insertion and action of this agent within cyberspace” <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 86)</2>, reinforcing that it is a form of hypervulnerability resulting from the sum of vulnerabilities beyond the usual, arising from the characteristics of this environment <3>Acosta</3><4>(Acosta, 2025, p. 93)</4>.

Among them, the aggravated technical vulnerability stands out, associated with two central circumstances: a structural one, linked to the very architecture of the virtual environment, and a situational one, related to the cognitive and behavioral effects produced in the use of this medium, both responsible for further weakening the consumer in digitally established relations <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 97)</2>.

In addition, he makes explicit other concrete factors that deepen this picture, such as the informational power gap, the lack of digital literacy, the indiscriminate collection and processing of personal data and the manipulation of individuals' will <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 120)</2>.

In an especially illuminating passage, the author describes how the digital market tends to condition the provision of services on data collection, the data being subsequently stored and processed by algorithms aimed at shaping will, whether through behavioral advertising or through broader forms of decision-inducement in favor of companies or of other centers of power that control such informational bases <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 83-84)</2>.

The author insists on the need to establish a concept and parameters based on the principles of the Consumer Protection Code and the Federal Constitution, precisely to allow effective protection and guarantee material equality to consumers inserted in cyberspace <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 93)</2>.

This appears when the author recognizes the precariousness, the near nonexistence, of normative protection specifically aimed at the “cybervulnerable”, which makes the direct subsumption of protective rules in the Brazilian legal system difficult and makes the search for provisional interpretive solutions inevitable <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 113)</2>.

The same tension reappears when he defends, for the future, specific regulation that recognizes and combats the aggravated vulnerabilities in cyberspace, while, in the present, resort is had to interpretation favorable to the consumer based on the CDC and the Constitution <1>Acosta</1><2>(Acosta, 2025, p. 119)</2>.

With Louis D. Brandeis he founded the firm Warren & Brandeis <1>(1879)</1>, predecessor of today's Nutter, McClennen & Fish.

Entitled The Right to Privacy, the seminal article by Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis <1>([201-?])</1>, originally published by the Harvard Law Review in 1890, formulates a matrix of legal reconstruction in the face of technical and social mutations that alter conditions of exposure, vulnerability and harm.

The recourse to Brandeis <1>(2011)</1> at this point serves a function of structural reinforcement of the diagnosis already established about the Lex Plataformae as practical normativity, avoiding both the moralization of private power and the statist leap.

In the arrangement described by Brandeis, domination does not impose itself as a formal public command, but as gradual control of essential circuits and as the capacity to coordinate decisions through the administration of other people's money <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 27])</2>.

In this register, decisive influence does not arise from wealth itself, but from the capacity to command the resources of others and, thereby, direct economic conduct and trajectories <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 37])</2>.

Brandeis describes how distinct functions indispensable to business end up gathered in the figure of the investment banker, and attributes to this gathering the formation of the Money Trust <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 26-27])</2>.

From there, the historical form of the phenomenon becomes comparable to that of political despotism, since it is established by progressive usurpation, with incremental advance and not by violent acts of rupture <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 26-27])</2>.

Brandeis is explicit as to the requirement of separation between banking activity and the financed business, because the accumulation of functions produces a structural conflict of interest <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 196])</2>.

The author describes this type of rationality by showing how the decision-maker may orient his action by the probable effect on market value, keeping permanent attention on how facts will be read by investors and by the street <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 200])</2>.

Entitled Other People’s Money and How the Bankers Use It, the work of Louis D. Brandeis <1>(2011)</1>, originally published between 1913 and 1914 as a series of articles in the periodical Harper’s Weekly, constitutes a structural critique of the formation of a financial oligarchy at the beginning of the twentieth century. Of interest here is solely the characterization of the legal-institutional mechanism described by Brandeis.

The point is not merely “one director on two boards”, but the network of ties that allows decisions and contracts to be conducted through crossed circuits, reducing decision-making independence and confusing fiduciary loyalties <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 67])</2>.

For him, when bigness is obtained through combinations and mergers and comes to be administered remotely, the result tends to be concentration of power with loss of decision-making quality and practical inability to govern operational complexity without degradation, which transforms “bigness” into a source of inefficiency and systemic risk <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 166])</2>.

Functional encroachment designates, in Brandeis, the way in which a financial oligarchy consolidates itself not by a single act of conquest, but by gradual, discreet and often barely visible usurpation, which progressively shifts to the same group functions that, when exercised separately, tend to produce reciprocal controls and competitive balance <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Brandeis, 2011, [p. 25-28])</2>.

Data are not neutral matter of market circulation, but legally relevant projections of personality, whose protection is linked to human dignity and informational self-determination <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155-156)</2>.
Luciana Lopes Canavez, Isadora Beatriz Magalhães Santos and Daniella Salvador Trigueiro Mendes

The information society itself, by intensifying private structures of surveillance and behavioral analysis, required the explicit statement of new fundamental rights and the reinforcement of data protection as a response to the practical erosion of privacy <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69-70; p. 78-79; p. 82- 83)</2>.

This means recognizing that private structures of digital governance bear on privacy, personality, freedom and self-determination with sufficient intensity to justify reinforced legal containment <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141; p. 152; p. 155)</2>.

Along the same lines, massive data exploitation, behavioral analysis and corporate surveillance show that these private powers today operate over central spheres of autonomy to a constitutionally relevant degree, requiring a more robust normative response <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70; p. 72; p. 78)</2>.

Along these lines, data protection imposes a true obligation on the processing agent to respect the data subject's informational self-determination, precisely because personal data constitute an extension of their personality, protected by the constitutional centrality of human dignity <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155)</2>.

The same key appears when it is stated that the guarantee of protection of personal data, whether through the discipline of the LGPD or through the incidence of the horizontal effect of fundamental rights in the concrete case, especially those linked to privacy and personality, ultimately aims at the protection of the fundamental rights of the data subject <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 156)</2>.

For this reason, the infraconstitutional protection of personal data can be understood as an expression of the mediate horizontal effect of the fundamental rights of freedom, privacy and free development of the natural person, opening space for a more direct incidence of these principles in private relations <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 156)</2>.

Along these lines, the development of information and communication technologies, in a surveillance society marked by the mitigation of privacy, imposed the need to reflect on new fundamental rights <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69-70)</2>.

The same key is reinforced when it is recognized that the economic exploitation of personal data without sufficient consent did not remain only at the infraconstitutional level, the case law of the STF having confirmed the existence of autonomous fundamental rights to the protection of personal data and to informational self-determination <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 82-83)</2>.

In addition, these rights are understood as the result of an evolutive interpretation of privacy, whose protection had to be reconfigured to remain effective in the surveillance society <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 78-79)</2>.

In this direction, the protection of personality rights is not exhausted by their positivization in the Civil Code, also having the stature of fundamental rights, which makes it possible to understand data protection itself as a form of defense of these rights <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 152)</2>.

The same reasoning is reinforced when the problem is situated in the tension between an impersonal market and the protection of the fundamental rights of the natural person subjected to such influences, from a perspective of repersonalization of private law <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141)</2>.

In cases of justifiable vulnerability, even the immediate use of the fundamental norm, in its pure form, is admitted to enable the effective rebalancing between the parties <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155)</2>.

In a surveillance society, the enormous quantity of personal data converted into information about personality and intimacy, and used by companies for behavioral analysis, calls into question the very possibility of preserving privacy <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>.

This reading deepens when it is recognized, in dialogue with Shoshana Zuboff, that the power derived from the extraction and analysis of personal data reaches the capacity to shape human behavior, requiring responses of containment and regulation of surveillance capitalism <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 72)</2>.

In addition, the existence of abuses committed by technology companies reinforces the need for more robust protection of data processing relations, including in digital media <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 78)</2>.

In the digital environment, storage, sharing and persistent monitoring of information represent a sufficiently serious threat to privacy to require specific normative containment, above all in a surveillance society in which data processing becomes a central asset of business models and behavioral control <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69; p. 73; p. 82)</2>.

The security argument itself may function as a legitimizer of the expansion of private powers over fundamental spheres of informational life, especially when the demand for data and structural surveillance are normalized by routine and barely intelligible acceptances <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70-71)</2>.

In the digital environment, the constant storage and sharing of information represent a serious threat to fundamental rights, especially privacy, requiring more specific regulatory action to impose limits on abuses of this nature <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69)</2>.

The same key is reinforced when contemporary society is described as a true surveillance society, permanently directed at data collection, which explains the need to regulate digital relations with a focus on the protection of personal data, privacy and other fundamental rights affected by this technological medium <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 73)</2>.

In addition, the processing of personal data has become the main asset of a hyperconnected society, serving as raw material for improving businesses and extracting behavioral patterns aimed at classifying and categorizing people, which is why Law seeks to keep pace with this development through new legislation and new rights aimed at safeguarding fundamental rights <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 82)</2>.

In the context following the September 11 attack, a gradual movement of mitigation of privacy and other fundamental guarantees was consolidated in the name of a growing need for transparency, opening space for companies to begin collecting, selecting and classifying personal data for the purpose of controlling individuals <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>.

The same logic appears when the use of platforms and websites is frequently conditioned on the entry of personal data, often without the data subject's effectively qualified consent, such data being subsequently exploited commercially and monetized through advertising and other business models <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>.

In reinforcement, automated processing not only knows human behavior, but shapes it at scale, so that the goal ceases to be merely automating the flow of information about people and comes to include the automation of people themselves <1>Mendes</1><2>(Zuboff apud Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 71)</2>.

The digital experience may reach legally relevant dimensions of personal integrity precisely because data protection, informational self-determination and free development of personality form part of the existential core of the person in the informational environment <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 139; p. 148; p. 155-156)</2>.

In contemporary terms, it means recognizing that so-called digital dossiers constitute a new type of identity and that personal data are connected to the free exercise and development of human personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141; p. 153)</2>.

Along these lines, the specific protection of personal data appears as a means of guaranteeing already enshrined fundamental rights, such as freedom and privacy, as well as others developed more recently, among them informational self-determination and the free development of personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 139)</2>.

This articulation deepens when it is stated that informational self-determination is directed precisely at the free development of the data subject's personality, which is why any interpretation that distorts it, for example through unrestricted consent harmful to this development, must be considered unacceptable <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 148)</2>.

In reinforcement, informational self-determination and the centrality of the data subject appear as means of enhancing the free determination and free development of the natural person's personality, giving them the instruments to control the processing of their data, including as to confirmation of the existence of processing, correction, modification and deletion <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155-156)</2>.

The repersonalization of private law, in this context, puts back at the center the tension between the demands of an impersonal, economically oriented market and the need to protect the fundamental rights of the natural person subjected to external influences <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141)</2>.

This reading gains density when it is recognized that data processing activities have growing interference in people's lives and that so-called digital dossiers constitute a “new type of identity”, which is why the correction of this information becomes essential for the data subject's identity to be projected faithfully, dogmatically justifying the inclusion of personal data in the category of personality rights <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 153)</2>.

In reinforcement, personal data are qualified as a “true extension of the free exercise and development of human personality”, so that informational self-determination is not justified by mere ownership of data, but by its indissoluble relation to the data subject's personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 153)</2>.

Warat makes this core explicit when he treats the semiology of power as an analysis of how signification can function as an instrument of social control, a normalizing and disciplinary strategy and a consensus-producing formula, capable of fabricating effects of verisimilitude about the material conditions of social life <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 18)</2>.

Objectively, the author maintains that the legitimacy of power depends on discursive work and can be obtained through adequate manipulation of words, which shifts the appearance of publicity and formal validity to the level of its strategic production <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 18)</2>.

This operation is reinforced when it is recognized that the stability of meaning is sustained by prior ideological coincidence, so that belief in normative univocity and in the unalterability of signifiers does not result from naivety, but functions as a condition of social effectiveness of the ideal of the rational legal norm <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 68)</2>.

For this reason, obedience can be produced without explicit command, since the social idiom tends to constitute an ordered subjectivity, allowing physical violence to be dispensed with and converting it into significative violence or imaginary violence, through which social cohesion is maintained by the creation of phantasmatic significations <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 110)</2>

Entitled O Direito e sua Linguagem, the work of Luis Alberto Warat <1>(1984)</1> directly introduces the problem of language in Law, setting aside the idea that legal discourse would operate as a neutral instrument of naming.

It is through its ‘devices of signification’ that power disciplines bodies, causing the members of a society to bind their desires to power. […] The ‘social idiom’ ends up constituting an ‘ordered subjectivity’ […] that allows physical violence to be progressively dispensed with, transformed into ‘significative violence’, into ‘imaginary violence’. […] Society keeps itself cohesive by resorting to the creation of phantasmatic significations […]” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1995, p. 110)</2>.

It is in this key that signification can be analyzed as an instrument of social control, of normalization and of consensus production, and not merely as a neutral vehicle of information <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>.
Hence the pertinence of abandoning environmental labels in favor of categories that isolate the effective mechanism of meaning production <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 15; p. 47)</2>.

Warat is explicit in stating that signification must be analyzed “as an instrument of social control”, “as a normalizing and disciplinary strategy of individuals”, “as a consensus-producing formula” and “as a persuasive power provoking effects of verisimilitude about the material conditions of social life” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>.

For the author, languages are not limited to the informative content they apparently transmit; they engender “significative and normalizing resonances of social practices”, inserting themselves into a deeper dynamic of “social production of meanings” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 15)</2>.

In a convergent sense, Warat observes that pragmatic analysis makes it possible to articulate functions such as “persuasion, legitimation, anticipation”, showing how certain discourses produce an “effect of unquestionability and reality about knowledge” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</2>.

Pragmatics applied to law makes it possible to perceive that ideology is “a factor inseparable from the conceptual structure made explicit in general norms”, requiring from the interpreter a reading that discovers “the connections between the words of the law and the political and ideological factors that produce and determine its functions in society” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 47)</2>.

Normative discourses involve a “game of persuasion and mythification” that stereotypes meanings and legitimizes the reproduction of power under the appearance of normality <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 45)</2>.

Through the use of “a language impregnated with stereotyped significations”, there is introduced, “under the supposed appearance of an objective description, an ideological dimension not formulated in legal language”, the central objective of these expressions being “to influence and determine opinions” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 71)</2>.

The “coherent organization of a discourse” can “silence problems” and, through these silences, fulfill “political functions in society”, at the same time as it “explicitly forces subjects to say or repress certain things” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 50)</2>.

This selectivity is reinforced when legal discourse presents itself under the appearance of univocity and closure: belief in normative univocity presupposes “prior ideological coincidence” and the unalterability of signifiers sustains the ideal of a rational norm precisely because it ensures certain “social effects of the law in society” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 68)</2>.

In criticizing the assertion of the closed character of legal language, it becomes evident that the requirements of totality and closure of the system are not simple logical requirements, but ideological representations that satisfy specific functions of the legal form <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 54)</2>.

Consensus on the legitimacy of power is the result of discursive work, which is effective precisely because it operates through “a game of stereotyping”, whose primary function is legitimation <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 18)</2>.

In this situation, physical violence becomes dispensable to a large extent, being replaced by “significative violence” and “imaginary violence”, capable of neutralizing the critical power of subjectivity and producing internalized obedience <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 110)</2>.

Certain effects of acceptance spread without the need for explicit demonstration, relying on stereotypes, topical formulas and already sedimented beliefs, so that discursive alignment spreads “like an infection” or “contagion” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 88)</2>.

The author warns that the function of domination should not be analyzed “from a psychologistic point of view”, since senders and receivers are institutionally situated and their discourses operate as supports of a mediatized ideology <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 67)</2>.

This key is reinforced when Warat shows that the producer of discourse can secure for himself “the monopoly of the constitution of the denotative field”, selecting designative properties for persuasive purposes and leaving receivers “dormant to the discussion of the persuasively proposed designative criteria” <1>Warat</1><2>(Warat, 1984, p. 70)</2>.

POSTMAN, Neil. <1>Amusing ourselves to death:</1> public discourse in the age of show business. New introduction by Andrew Postman. 20th anniversary ed. New York: Penguin Books, 2006.
The contribution of Neil Postman <1>(2006)</1>, influenced by Ellul, shifts the technical diagnosis to the level of media as the dominant cultural form.

Politics, religion and education come to operate under the grammar of entertainment, in a society that approaches the condition of “amusing ourselves to death” <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</2>.

In the political field, visual logic shifts the weight of argument to appearance, performance and impression management, reducing the centrality of programs, ideologies and substantive confrontations of ideas <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</2>.
In the religious domain, television tends to convert the experience of transcendence into spectacle, emptying ritual density and symbolic depth <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</2>.

In education, a pedagogical philosophy oriented by immediate accessibility and contentment is consolidated, to the detriment of cognitive effort and more demanding intellectual formation <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 96])</2>.
Postman <1>(2006)</1> makes it possible to understand media as a form of organization of social knowledge, and not merely as a channel for the circulation of messages.

The passage from typographic culture to television did not alter only the communicational medium; it transformed criteria of truth, intelligence and seriousness in public discourse <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 23])</2>.

Under this regime, television favors fragmentation, reduces the possibility of more complex discourses and replaces the argumentative coherence of typographic culture with public conversations marked by triviality, by rupture of sequence and by the progressive abandonment of logic, reason and rules of contradiction <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58])</2>.
For Postman, television reconfigures it as a branch of show business, transforming public debate into a product compatible with entertainment <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 16])</2>.
In this context, “knowing” politics comes to mean visual familiarity, and not necessarily understanding structured by language and discourse <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 86])</2>.

The critical and in-depth process loses space to recreational forms of access to content, while difficulty, intellectual discipline and the duration of cognitive effort come to be seen as obstacles to efficient communication <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 146])</2>.

Hence the assertion that television and image culture do not constitute merely a style of communication, but a threat to the foundations of liberal democracy, insofar as they strike its material basis: freedom of information <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 91])</2>.

The image dismembers reality by tearing moments from their contexts and juxtaposing events without logical or historical connection, recreating the world as a series of idiosyncratic happenings <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 55])</2>.

In this environment, intelligence comes to mean knowing of many things, and not knowing about them, that is, accumulating disconnected data without in-depth understanding <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 74])</2>.

Disinformation, therefore, is not reducible to falsehood; since it also manifests itself as misplaced, irrelevant, fragmented or superficial information, capable of producing an illusion of knowledge and distancing the subject from effective knowing <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 74])</2>.

This form of informational circulation produces a present without historicity, in which television operates as a medium centered on the now and makes it difficult to integrate experience into a broader temporal narrative <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 76])</2>.

Public discourse thus loses the form that made it fit for rationality: under print culture, it tended toward coherence, seriousness and continuity; under televisual governance, it comes to be organized by visuality, brevity and the demand for immediate interest <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 65-66])</2>.

Information is presented in simplified, insubstantial and decontextualized form, not necessarily through explicit censorship, but because television operates as a meta-medium, directing both what is known of the world and the social ways of knowing <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58])</2>.

From this change of base, politics, religion, news, education and commerce come to be rearranged as congenial adjuncts of show business, and culture tends to become a generalized arena of entertainment <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 58-59])</2>.

In this key, the contemporary threat to democracy need not take the form of censorship, since it is realized when political discourse takes the form of entertainment and neutralizes the very seriousness of public debate <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 91-93])</2>.

By shifting the center of discourse to performance, the medium lowers the public centrality of substantive themes and weakens the social conditions of critical thought, above all when information is presented in a simplistic and non-contextual way, that is, as information packaged as entertainment <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 92])</2>.

Influenced by the theory of Jacques Ellul, in the work Amusing Ourselves to Death: Public Discourse in the Age of Show Business (“Divertindo-nos até a morte: o discurso público na era do show business”, in our translation), originally published in 1985, the American educator Neil Postman <1>(2006)</1> investigates the influence of television on American culture, exploring the ways in which television, by assuming the condition of dominant means of communication, transformed public discourse into entertainment and deeply affected the social, cultural and political epistemologies of the USA.

In the religious field, Postman maintains that television converts religion, without ceremony, into entertainment, removing what made it a historical, profound and sacred practice, with loss of ritual, dogma, tradition, theology and, above all, spiritual transcendence <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</2>.
In this formatting, preachers cease to be mere mediators and come to function as media protagonists, so that “their featured players become celebrities” <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 82])</2>.
The author describes this shift with explicit irony when he says that, in these programs, “the preacher is tops” and “God comes out as second banana” <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 79])</2>.

God “exists only in our minds”, while the preacher is “there, to be seen, admired, adored”, becoming the star of the show under an essentially structural logic <1>Postman</1><2>(Postman, 2006, [p. 83])</2>.

Postman's final contribution lies in a warning about the dangers of the "distracted society" that the communication mechanism had created, a concept that resonates forcefully in the contemporary context, in which the reality observed by Postman <1>(2006)</1> was raised to exponentiality through the insertion of new digital communication technologies that only asserted and amplified the dynamics previously observed by the author.
